title: Animal bite: first aid and rabies
asks: bitten by a wild animal what do i do
a dog bit me do i need a rabies shot
how long should i wash an animal bite
the bite was a while ago is it too late for rabies treatment
should i catch or kill the animal that bit me
bit by a stray dog wat now
animal bite, skin is broken, far from a hospital, what do we do, over
answer: Get away from the animal first. Remove yourself from further harm, and make sure you are no longer at risk of being bitten again.
Control bleeding: apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce bleeding.

Clean the wound: rinse it thoroughly with clean water or saline solution, and gently remove any debris using mild soap and water. Because of rabies, the Army field sanitation manual says that cleaning the wound or exposure site with soap and water for at least 15 minutes is the most important first step in treatment.
If animal saliva got on broken skin or in your eyes or mouth, immediately wash that area with soap and water too.

Then consider an antiseptic; the sources differ. The Army first aid manual says to apply an antiseptic solution or ointment that is suitable for use on open wounds, following the instructions on its label. The JTS wound-care guideline says additives such as iodine, bacitracin or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection.
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing or clean bandage, and change the dressing regularly.

Get medical evaluation for every animal bite, and seek it immediately: especially bites from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or wounds that become red, swollen or increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the bite, prescribe antibiotics if necessary, and give tetanus prophylaxis if required.

Ask about rabies treatment: with any animal bite, rabies is the primary concern. The Army first aid manual says that unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the person bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. The older HHS ship's medical manual says rabies treatment can usually be withheld after a provoked bite by a domestic dog or cat, if the animal is available for observation and appears healthy over a 10 day period; it adds that a dog or cat that bites without apparent provocation may be considered rabid, and that each case must be analyzed carefully.

Do not wait: the Army field sanitation manual says that when medical treatment is obtained promptly after a rabies exposure, nearly all cases of rabies will be prevented. If time has already passed since a bite or other exposure, still get evaluated: the same manual says older exposures still require evaluation, and treatment if required.

Report the animal: give medical personnel any information that will help identify it. The Army first aid manual says to do this if you are unable to capture or kill the animal. The Army field sanitation manual says capturing animals for observation, or euthanizing them for rabies testing, is best performed by qualified veterinary or health-protection personnel who are already vaccinated against the disease, and that failure to follow proper procedures can result in greater exposure to rabies.
warnings: You cannot always tell if an animal has rabies. Once the signs and symptoms of rabies develop, the disease is almost always fatal. Rabies is preventable if an exposed person receives prompt medical care.
Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, and the bite from a mammal can cause a severe infection.
Suturing is rarely appropriate for bite or puncture wounds: it can increase the risk of infection.

quotes.text: First aid for human or animal bites aims to prevent infection and provide initial care for the wound. To perform first aid for a human or animal bite: Remove yourself from further harm. If dealing with an animal bite, ensure that you are no longer at risk of being bitten again. Control bleeding. If the bite wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze to stop or minimize the bleeding. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce bleeding.

Clean the wound. Rinse the bite wound thoroughly with clean water or saline solution to flush out any dirt, bacteria, or saliva that may have entered the wound. Gently remove any debris from the wound using mild soap and water. Apply an antiseptic. After cleaning, apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound to help reduce the risk of infection. Follow the instructions on the product label and ensure it is suitable for use on open wounds. Cover the wound. Use a sterile dressing or clean bandage to cover the wound. This will protect it from further contamination and promote healing. Change dressing regularly to maintain cleanliness.

When medical treatment is obtained promptly following a rabies exposure, nearly all cases of rabies will be prevented. Cleaning of the wound or exposure site with soap and water for at least 15 minutes is the most important first step in treatment, followed by administration of postexposure prophylaxis. Postexposure prophylaxis is still effective if given weeks, months, or even years after a potential exposure, so older exposures still require evaluation and, if required, treatment with postexposure prophylaxis.

If you are bitten or get animal saliva on broken skin or in your eyes or mouth, immediately wash the area with soap and water and seek immediate medical attention. Rabies is preventable if exposed individuals receive prompt medical care after being exposed.
Additives such as iodine, bacitracin, or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection.

Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the severity of the bite, prescribe antibiotics if necessary, and administer tetanus prophylaxis if required.
All individuals who may have been exposed to an animal bite or saliva should seek immediate medical evaluation and treatment.
It is important to report and seek evaluation for all animal exposures regardless of how the animal was behaving.

If someone gets bitten by an animal, whether known, unknown, wild, or domestic, the primary concern is rabies. Unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the individual who has been bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, so it is essential to consult a health care professional to determine the appropriate course of action and receive any necessary medical treatment.

Most bites by domestic dogs and cats are provoked. If the history indicates this, usually rabies treatment can be withheld, if the animal is available for observation, and appears to be healthy over a 10 day period. However, the dog or cat that bites without apparent provocation may be considered rabid. Each case must be analyzed carefully before a conclusion can be reached on whether or not to proceed with treatment.
If unable to capture or kill the animal, provide medical personnel with any information that will help identify it.

Capturing animals for observation or euthanizing animals for rabies testing is best performed by qualified veterinary or force health protection personnel who are already vaccinated against the disease.
Note. Failure to follow proper procedures can result in greater potential exposure to rabies.
You cannot always tell if an animal has rabies. Once the signs and symptoms of rabies develop, the disease is almost always fatal in man.
Take caution, mammals have teeth and will bite in self-defense. The bite from a mammal can cause a severe infection.

Immediate shipside wound care includes cleansing and irrigation to remove as many microorganisms (including rabies virus) as possible. Soap and water, or saline solution, can be used. Suturing is rarely appropriate for bite or puncture wounds since it can increase the risk of infection.

conflict: New card (2026-11-25): the bite first aid split off from dangerous-animals-encounter as a protocol, as the reviewer asked; lines, quotes and conflicts carried over, with the reviewer's fixes. (1) Who needs rabies treatment (shown side by side in step 8): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 16-6 says the person bitten 'must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine' unless the animal is someone's pet verified up to date on rabies, and ATP 4-25.12 para 6-49 says to seek evaluation for all animal exposures 'regardless of how the animal was behaving'; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) says treatment can usually be withheld after a provoked bite by a domestic dog or cat that stays healthy over a 10 day observation period, and (added in revision) 'However, the dog or cat that bites without apparent provocation may be considered rabid.' The owner must choose. (2) The biting animal (step 10 now shows ATP 4-25.12 beside ATP 4-02.11): ATP 4-25.12 says capturing or euthanizing an animal for rabies testing 'is best performed by qualified veterinary or force health protection personnel who are already vaccinated against the disease' and that if the animal is killed its intact head should go, packed in ice, to a veterinary or medical laboratory; ATP 4-02.11 only says what to do 'If unable to capture or kill the animal'. Not shown as an instruction, for the owner to decide: the HHS manual says domestic dogs and cats that bite 'should be captured and observed for signs of rabies for the 10 days' and that any wild mammalian carnivore or bat that bites or scratches a person 'should be humanely killed at once' with the head kept refrigerated for a public health laboratory; the card shows HHS's 10-day observation only as its condition for withholding treatment. (3) Wound washing: ATP 4-25.12 says soap and water for at least 15 minutes; ATP 4-02.11 and the HHS manual give no time. (4) Antiseptic on the bite (shown in step 5): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says 'apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound'; the JTS Wound Management guideline (2017) says 'Additives such as iodine, bacitracin, or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection'. (5) Wording, per the reviewer: ATP 4-25.12's 'still effective if given weeks, months, or even years after a potential exposure' is given in step 9 as 'if time has already passed, still get evaluated', after the prompt-treatment sentence, so that it does not read as 'no hurry'; the full sentence is in the quote.
